question: What specific cells in the human body does HIV primarily attack and destroy?
explanation: HIV specifically targets and destroys CD4+ T-lymphocytes, which weakens the immune response over time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h1)

question: What is the main difference between HIV and AIDS?

options.A: HIV only affects children whereas AIDS affects adults.
options.B: HIV is transmitted by blood while AIDS is transmitted sexually.
options.C: AIDS can be cured completely with antibiotics unlike HIV.
options.D: AIDS is the advanced stage when the immune system is severely damaged.

explanation: Think of HIV as the virus that enters the body, and AIDS as the later stage when the immune system gets very weak and can no longer fight off sickness. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which enzyme helps HIV convert its viral RNA into DNA inside the host cell?
explanation: HIV uses an enzyme called reverse transcriptase to rewrite its genetic code from RNA into DNA so it can hide inside our body's cells. Clever little virus, but now you know its trick! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h2)

question: Which of the following is NOT a primary mode of HIV transmission?

options.A: Unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected person
options.B: Sharing contaminated needles among drug users
options.C: Casual social contact like hugging and sharing utensils
options.D: Transmission from an infected mother to her baby during birth

explanation: HIV is not spread through everyday casual social contact, sweat, tears, saliva, or insect bites. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h2)

question: What happens during the clinical latency stage of HIV?

options.A: The immune system completely eradicates the virus without treatment.
options.B: The virus multiplies slowly and the patient often feels healthy.
options.C: CD4 cell counts rapidly increase above normal levels.
options.D: The patient experiences severe opportunistic infections immediately.

explanation: During this quiet period, the virus stays active but multiplies slowly. Many patients look and feel completely fine, which is why testing is so important! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h3)

question: A patient is officially diagnosed with AIDS when their CD4 count drops below which threshold?
explanation: A CD4 count falling below 200 cells/mm3 marks the transition from chronic HIV infection to a diagnosis of AIDS. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h3)

question: Within how many hours must Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) be started to work effectively?
explanation: Time is precious here! PEP needs to start as soon as possible, and ideally within 72 hours after a possible exposure, to stop the virus from taking root. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h4)

question: How does Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) help prevent HIV?

options.A: It is given as a one-time vaccine to provide lifelong immunity.
options.B: It is taken only after a person knows they have been exposed to the virus.
options.C: It kills existing opportunistic infections in AIDS patients.
options.D: It is taken daily by HIV-negative people to block the virus from establishing an infection.

explanation: Think of PrEP as a daily shield. People who are HIV-negative take it regularly to keep the virus from setting up shop if exposure happens. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h4)

question: What does the acronym VCT stand for in HIV nursing care?
explanation: VCT stands for Voluntary Counseling and Testing, a core strategy for encouraging people to know their HIV status confidentially. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h5)

question: A patient tests positive for HIV at the clinic. What is your best immediate nursing action?

options.A: Report the patient's name to local community leaders immediately
options.B: Advise the patient to stop working and isolate at home forever
options.C: Provide compassionate post-test counseling and link the patient to treatment services
options.D: Wait until the patient asks questions before saying anything about treatment

explanation: A positive test can be scary. As a nurse, your warmth, privacy, and gentle guidance are vital to connect them straight to the care they need. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h5)

question: What is the main goal of Antiretroviral Therapy (ART)?

options.A: To suppress viral replication and reduce the viral load to undetectable levels
options.B: To prevent bacterial infections like pneumonia and tuberculosis
options.C: To completely eliminate the HIV virus from every cell in the body
options.D: To cure advanced stages of AIDS within two weeks of treatment

explanation: While ART doesn't clear every single trace of the virus, it puts a heavy brake on it, lowering the viral load so the immune system can bounce back and stay strong. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h6)

question: Why is taking ART medications every single day so important for patients?

options.A: Missing a single dose causes immediate death from opportunistic infections.
options.B: Inconsistent taking of drugs can cause the virus to mutate and develop resistance to treatment.
options.C: Taking pills at irregular times makes the medication taste much worse.
options.D: Strict adherence is only necessary during the first month of therapy.

explanation: Consistency is key! If a patient skips doses, drug levels drop in the blood, giving the crafty virus a chance to change its form and beat the medicine. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h6)

question: What does PMTCT stand for in maternal and child health nursing?

options.B: Primary Medical Treatment and Care Techniques
options.C: Pediatric Medication Testing and Clinical Trials

explanation: PMTCT stands for Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission, which encompasses strategies to stop vertical HIV spread during pregnancy, birth, and breastfeeding. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h7)

question: When should an HIV-positive pregnant woman start taking ART under PMTCT guidelines?

options.A: Only if she develops symptoms of full-blown AIDS
options.B: Immediately upon diagnosis, regardless of CD4 count
options.C: Only after the baby is successfully delivered
options.D: Only during the final month of pregnancy

explanation: Starting ART right away helps drop the mother's viral load as low as possible, giving her baby the best shield of protection before birth. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h7)

question: What is the most common opportunistic infection and leading cause of death in people with HIV?
explanation: Tuberculosis (TB) is the top opportunistic infection we watch out for in patients with weakened immune systems. Catching it early saves lives! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h8)

question: Why do patients with advanced HIV easily catch opportunistic infections?

options.A: Their red blood cell count drops too low to carry oxygen.
options.B: Antiretroviral medications cause bacterial infections as a side effect.
options.C: Their damaged immune systems cannot fight off germs that healthy bodies easily control.
options.D: They live in environments with too many synthetic chemicals.

explanation: When CD4 cells are low, the body's security guard is down. Germs that wouldn't normally bother a healthy person can easily cause trouble. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h8)

question: What is a major negative effect of HIV-related stigma in our communities?

options.A: It eliminates the need for VCT clinics.
options.B: It discourages people from getting tested or seeking treatment.
options.C: It increases the effectiveness of antiretroviral drugs.
options.D: It causes the HIV virus to mutate into a weaker strain.

explanation: Fear of being judged makes people hide their status and stay away from clinics. Compassion and education are our best tools to fight this stigma! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h9)

question: How do home-based care programs help patients with advanced HIV disease?

options.A: By diagnosing new infectious diseases without laboratory testing equipment
options.B: By replacing the need for antiretroviral medications entirely with herbal remedies
options.C: By providing family-supported nursing care, hygiene assistance, and monitoring at home
options.D: By isolating patients from their families so they never leave the bedroom

explanation: Home-based care brings comfort right to the doorstep, helping families manage daily nursing care, hygiene, and spotting any new symptoms early. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h9)
